[quote=lavinsworth_united_islands;58674221][b]Lavian Intervention in The Swabati Revolution[/b] (expansion and lore post)

[spoiler][b][i]EXCERPT FROM: Curiosity Textbooks: Lavian History and Geopolitical Relations[/i] [/b]

By 1886, relations between Greater Lavia and Swabati were at an all-time high. Lavian experts had been sent to help modernize Swabati and in return, King Kavavenga allowed special privileges to Lavian ships, as well as allowing for a small garrison and fort near the capital city. However, this introduction of modern political thought and ideas to Swabati had consequences, the chief of which was Dovane Brenit, the son of King Kavavenga. He had gotten his fathers permission to travel to any country he wanted for education, and he chose an Albic university. During his time in Albany, he became heavily influenced by communist ideology and created the Swabati Revolutionary
Workers Party (SRWP) while abroad. In 1889, he returned to Swabati with a few of his new party members, and intent to topple the kingdom. 

	Spending roughly a year influencing many sections of the country, Brenit managed to acquire quite a few followers, including multiple guards of the royal palace. On September 10th, 1889, he and members of the SRWP stormed the palace and with the help of collaborators in the royal guards, took over the palace and captured King Kavavenga, Queen Tralpon, as well as Prince Salcota. The whole of the royal family was captured (or in charge of the coup) other than Princess Owana, who was in Greater Lavia to attend university there. With cells of SRWP members congregating in the capital of Omehama, the rebels overran police forces and captured the city along with two major forts and multiple armories. In two days, the rebel forces overtook the main island Madero and set siege to the Lavian Brenard Fort using captured weapons and their newly made Peoples army. 

On September 13th, the same day Sir Lavinsworth learned of the revolution, Brenit proclaimed the establishment of the Union of Swabati Workers and Common Men (USWCM). As the news swept over Greater Lavia, Princess Owana was immediately escorted to Primank island and placed under utmost protection. A small naval convoy of two cruisers and three destroyers was dispatched to Brenard Fort to resupply the defenders and provide fire support. Troops were quickly mustered, and the following day saw the departure of 60,000 men. The arrival of the convoy was met with great relief to the defenders, but the revolutionaries saw it as a direct escalation of the war. Brenit sent out a messenger to the fort and its defenders offering them to surrender for safe passage back home and a small amount of compensation for every casualty, but due to him still marking the letter the messenger carried with the royal seal, the messenger was held up at a checkpoint, arrested, and then shot on the charge of trying to help the royal family escape.

The day after, Brenit departed the palace to speak to a small force headed to another island, leaving the royal family in the hands of his most trusted and zealous party members. After the departure, word reached the palace of the messengers supposed crime, and the guards there decided to take drastic action. On September 18, 1889, guards entered the room where they were holding the royal family and executed them by firing squad. The news was spread fast and it did its job; it fueled the fire of the revolution. The news came to Brenit as not of celebration, but of doom. It came as a shock to him and sent him into a mental spiral, as evident in writings found in the palace after the war, Brenit stated that he saw holding the royal family as a way to have a somewhat legitimate claim to the country and keep his mental state together even through what he saw as horrible but necessary. In his own words, The holding of my family is a pitiful endeavor indeed, but it is a necessary one. We can not afford their escape and chance for them to mount an effective resistance, one that will surely be backed by others in the world. Simultaneously we can not afford for them to be abused in any way, lest my mind lose me and the world sees us as barbaric for their harm. Some would like to see them hang, which I find an extreme application of my philosophy and one I disagree with, but the fervor of radicals is seldomly close to reason. Throughout this war, I cannot allow such a cost to the workers and people of this nation for them to have to die for their freedom with the loss of my own family alongside the legitimacy of our newly found nation. 

Due to the efforts of Swabati loyalists on the mainland of West Shamat and many islands, as well as the Lavian fleet, the forces of the SRWP were mainly contained to the islands surrounding Balkio Madra. The ULR and remaining Swabati forces used three months to plan an invasion while small forces of elite Swabati jungle soldiers made small incursions to scout and disrupt SWRP activities, effectively becoming the first deployment of rudimentary special forces. After careful planning and an infiltration mission, members of the jungle rifles managed to assassinate Brenit on January 2nd, 1890. The assassination was the last step in preparation for the invasion of the SWRP-held islands, and the news of the successful mission triggered an immediate bombardment of revolutionary-held military installations, as well as landings on the four SWRP-held islands around Balkio Madra. These battles each took roughly a month respectively, allowing for the two-pronged invasion of the Swabati capital island on February 16th, 1890. Despite the overwhelming numbers of the Lavian army and the specialized forces of the Swabati loyalists, the invasion of the capital island evolved into a 5-month long struggle marked by guerilla warfare and violent urban fighting. This part of the campaign showed that even with its leader dead, multiple members of the SWRP were still competent in their roles. 

However, the struggles of the SWRP were in vain. By July, Lavian forces had successfully broken through the defenses of the remaining SWRP fighters and captured the capitol, the last beacon of resistance for the revolutionary forces on July 23rd, 1890. While there were still some pockets of resistance, this is considered by any the end of the Swabati rebellion. With the crowning of Princess Owana Tralpon (she gave herself her last name while under protection in Greater Lavia to honor her mother) as Queen Owana in September of 1890, the Swabati kingdom had made a full return, although under much more Lavian influence than before. This would be a precursor to the marriage of Herman Lavinsworth and Queen Owana in 1897, effectively integrating the Swabati kingdom into Greater Lavia.[/spoiler][/quote]

[b]Senate Hall: March 4th, 2025[/b]

The great marble hall of the North Thýven sat enshrouded in a dark gloom, punctured only by the oculus which shone a single beam of circular light down onto the marble floor. Arranged in a circle were 7 seats, with 7 senators, representing 7 states. 

Tensions had been high in the Senate as the President, Consantin Ptolenos VI, had been increasingly attempting to increase his powers over the legislature. Thankfully the supreme court had managed to halt any broad attempts at such movements, despite the clear familial relation to Consantin VI by head justice Doma Alexandrii-Claudis who was for all intents and purposes a distant cousin by marriage to the president. 

Nevertheless Consantin had continued his assault against the independence of the legislature leading to mutters from the Chamber of the Peoples that a recall of his office was very much necessary to preserve the stability of the republic.

It was this that the Senate had gathered to discuss  that Tuesday on March 4th, the question was clear but the aims and final goal was not.

The Senate shall come to order, stated the voice of the Speaker of the Senate Tito Alexandrii-Claudis (the brother of Doma). 

All the Senators who had been muttering along the sidelines of the circular hall moved slowly and begrudgingly to their seats, their robes swishing gently as they sat themselves, frowns appearing on their faces as if they were trying to get into the mood of unpleasant discourse.

Todays matter of business, gentlemen, shall be the proposal for a recall election as laid out by the Chamber of the Peoples, Stated Tito moving to seat himself at the marble seat that sat slightly raised, indicating his position as speaker, Discussion may begin, he stated following his being seated therein. 

The first senator, senator Eddwin Ettes rose to speak, Gentlemen, the republic is in danger, the tyranny of the dynastic presidency stands at its highest peak, and the people are now oft straining against it. I hold that if we order this recall, this would be the toppling of the dynastic presidency. he stated. 

Another senator, senator Caudis Sollón rose and declared, It is necessary gentlemen to consider the matter of stability, a recall so close to an election would be disastrous to public and legislative stability, especially so close to a convening of the Chamber of Unity, he stated. 

Yes senator Sollón, however, we cannot wait two more months for the president to completely usurp the powers of the people over his position, stated a third senator, senator Orles Giatés. 

Hark! What is the beguiling talk about usurpation, was not the crisis of 2000 not enough to show that the presidency cannot usurp the powers of the people? Did not the challenger Zoë Alexandrii find herself defeated by the nature of her chosen successor Vesos? enquired a fourth senator, senator Gollan Petronys. 

My dear senator, the crisis of 2000 revolved around a controversial cousin marriage by Vesos, who married his third cousin, this was seen as a moral outrage, replied Eddwin Ettes, This is not the same thing, and to compare this matter of tyranny to the familial drama of 2000 is a broad leap of logic, surely governor Essos did not appoint you to your seat to make such illogical claims about historical events? he challenged.

Gentlemen, why do we worry about matters of the past, when the present is more pressing? enquired Tito.

We worry, for the past is representative of the present, replied Gollan.

Nay, he worries because of his deep pockets, of which I am sure his hands are deep within, and wherein if we searched the coin of the president wouldst be found, replied a fifth senator, senator Alexander Mekedii. 

A brash accusation from one so young senator Alexander, replied Gollan sternly. 

Gentlemen, we must return to the matter at hand, do we, or do we not approve of the recall? stated Orles, slightly frustrated at the topic change. 

I say that we decline to accept the Chamber of the Peoples demand, it is too early and too close to the last election, the evidence is not yet compiled high enough to constitute a proper recall, replied Gollan. 

But to withhold our hand in the cause of justice, began Claudis, before being interrupted by Alexander.

Is to pervert and cause disaster, Alexander stated snarkily, yes, yes, we know your slogan Claudis, it was very well for the ilk kin of governor Titus, who appointed you therein to your seat, gave you his wife did he not? Now talk of corruption! HA! 

Hold your tongue young one, lest I cut it off and display it to my enemies, replied Claudis rising angrily, his hand moving to a fold in his robes.

A low murmur went through the room as the threat was made, causing the speaker to raise his 
hand to silence them before speaking, Gentlemen please, let us not descend into rabble and violence, it is not prudent, nor wise, nor becoming of our stature, please Claudis, hold your tongue, and that to you Alexander as well, he stated sternly, his eyes passing from Claudis to Alexander. 

Claudis silently sat down, a sneer tossed at Alexander as the muttering continued.

Now then, began Tito, Are there any further comments on this matter? he enquired.

Silence reigned over the hall as the senators said nothing. 

Very well then, shall we cast a quorum vote? enquired Tito, opening a tally book to record the vote. 

A few nods here and there.

Very good, let us vote. All in favor of the recall? he looked up and made note of the count, 3 in favor, he frowned.

Let us make another vote, all against? he looked up once more as he noted 3 against, his frown deepened. A few mutters rippled among the senators as it became clear that a tie had been made. 

Very well then, in accordance with constitutional principles, I, as speaker of the senate, shall cast the tie breaking vote. The vote with which I cast shall be against the recall, therefore it is 4 against and 3 for, stated Tito as Ettes, Giatés, and Mekedii rose up in anger shouting at Tito. 

HEAR HEAR, the despot has made his voice clear! roared Ettes, drawing his dagger from his robes as Alexander rushed to placate his fellow senator. Immediately as the chaos started guards rushed in from the darkened parts of the room where they placed a wall between the angered senators and speaker Tito, who was escorted quickly from the hall, visibly shaken by the ordeal. 

The chaos continued for a little against the guards, however, the raucous senators, quickly pacified by their fellow senators, made their way out of the hall, towards the place of the Chamber of the Peoples, which was in session. Despite the guards attempts to halt them, they burst into the great hall which was peacefully in session, Senator Alexander, declared loudly,

HEAR HEAR O PEOPLE OF THIS OUR GREAT REPUBLIC! THE DESPOT HAS SPOKEN! THE PRESIDENT WILL NOT BE RECALLED! he roared as confused members of the chamber turned to stare at the interruption to the senate.

What is that my good sir? enquired the prelate of the chamber of the peoples.

My good sir, " stated Ettes, "there was a tie in our hall and the despot, of whom you know the name of, cast his vote and the vote against the president failed to reach quorum, he said as he walked to the desk of the prelate. 

Is this how it is done? the prelate enquired, Was our constitution abused in such a manner that you have sought to stir the hearts and actions of our chamber? What violence men do you seek to bring here! he declared. 

I apologise for my voice, replied Alexander, It was unbecoming of my name, forgive me, he continued, bowing slightly.

Yet, sighed the prelate, You make a point here my good sir, the speaker of the senate has caused such a stir, tell me, by what blood is he? he enquired. 

He is the brother of the chief justice, Doma, replied Ette.

And by what means did he find himself to be the speaker? enquired the prelate.

Through vote, I believe, replied Giatés interjecting. 

Very well, I shall convene a vote here in this chamber to see whether we find this vote by the senate to be contestable, he replied wearily.

Very good sir, very good, replied Alexander, his blonde curls bouncing slightly. 

Now gentlemen, have you any other discourse, if not, please let this chamber do its duties, stated the prelate sternly. 

The senators all bowed and left the chamber, the silent eyes of the chamber staring back at them with slight disdain at having their proceedings interrupted so loudly.
